data.title: Spiral Matrix
data.summary:
Input: A 2D integer list matrix
Output: A 1D list containing all elements of the matrix traversed in spiral order starting from the top-left element
Rules: Traverse elements in the order: top row left-to-right, right column top-to-bottom, bottom row right-to-left, and left column bottom-to-top, repeating inward until all elements are visited.

data.key_insight: Maintain four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) representing the current unvisited rectangular layer of the matrix. As we traverse each side, shrink the respective boundary inward until boundaries cross.

steps.title: Initialize Boundaries and Result
steps.detail: Handle edge cases where the matrix is empty. Set top=0, bottom=len(matrix)-1, left=0, and right=len(matrix[0])-1. Create an empty list to store the spiral order.

steps.title: Traverse Top Row
steps.detail: Traverse from left to right along the top row. Then increment top by 1. If top > bottom, break.

steps.title: Traverse Right Column
steps.detail: Traverse from top to bottom along the right column. Then decrement right by 1. If left > right, break.

steps.title: Traverse Bottom Row
steps.detail: Traverse from right to left along the bottom row. Then decrement bottom by 1. If top > bottom, break.

steps.title: Traverse Left Column
steps.detail: Traverse from bottom to top along the left column. Then increment left by 1. If left > right, break.

data.space_complexity: O(1) auxiliary space excluding the output list

data.pattern_summary: Maintain active boundaries that restrict the search space or traversal area, shrinking them inward as outer layers are fully processed.

pattern_options.name: Boundary Shrinking
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We track four directional boundaries and shrink them inward after traversing each outer edge.

pattern_options.name: Depth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. DFS explores paths deeply and backtracks, which does not match the systematic layer-by-layer traversal of a spiral.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic Programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. DP solves problems by combining optimal subsolutions, whereas this requires a direct simulation of matrix coordinates.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While pointers are used to track boundaries, the movement follows a 2D perimeter loop rather than shrinking a linear sequence.

data.brute_force_idea: Simulate the traversal step-by-step by keeping track of the current top, bottom, left, and right boundaries, and moving along the four edges in sequence.
data.brute_force_why: Every single element in the m by n matrix is visited exactly once.
data.bottleneck: There is no wasted work. Every element in the matrix must be read at least once to form the output list, making O(m * n) time complexity the absolute theoretical limit.

Realize that any correct algorithm must touch all m times n elements, meaning the linear scan is already optimal.

data.overview: The spiral matrix algorithm traverses a 2D matrix in a clockwise spiral order by maintaining four boundary pointers (top, bottom, left, right). As each edge of the matrix is traversed, the corresponding boundary is shrunk inward until all elements are visited.
data.intuition: Imagine peeling an onion layer by layer. You walk along the top edge from left to right, down the right edge, across the bottom edge from right to left, and finally up the left edge, repeating the process for the inner sub-matrix.

flow_nodes.label: Initialize boundaries
flow_nodes.detail: Check if matrix is empty and set top, bottom, left, right.

flow_nodes.label: While top <= bottom and left <= right
flow_nodes.detail: Continue outer loop as long as there are unvisited rows and columns.

flow_nodes.label: Traverse top row, top++
flow_nodes.detail: Traverse from left to right along the top row and increment top.

flow_nodes.label: Traverse right col, right--
flow_nodes.detail: Traverse from top to bottom down the right column and decrement right.

flow_nodes.label: Check top <= bottom
flow_nodes.detail: Verify if bottom row still exists before traversing right to left.

flow_nodes.label: Traverse bottom row, bottom--
flow_nodes.detail: Traverse from right to left along the bottom row and decrement bottom.

flow_nodes.label: Check left <= right
flow_nodes.detail: Verify if left column still exists before traversing bottom to top.

flow_nodes.label: Traverse left col, left++
flow_nodes.detail: Traverse from bottom to top up the left column and increment left.

flow_nodes.label: Return result
flow_nodes.detail: Return the final 1D list containing all spiral elements.

pitfalls: Failing to check if top <= bottom or left <= right before traversing the bottom row and left column, leading to duplicate elements in single row or column matrices.
Incorrectly updating boundary variables after traversing each side.
Off-by-one errors in range limits when looping through rows and columns.

data.insight: The boundary shrinking approach removes the need for visited sets or complex directional state machines by tracking four strict limits: top, bottom, left, and right. As each edge of the matrix is fully traversed, the corresponding boundary moves inward. This guarantees that every cell is visited exactly once without overlap or redundant checks.

derivation.note: The while loop runs until the row and column boundaries cross, which happens in approximately (m + n) / 2 steps.
Iterates across the top row from left to right.
Iterates backward across the bottom row.
Iterates upward along the leftmost column.

data.time_summary: Every single element in the m x n matrix is visited and appended to the result list exactly once. Summing the steps across all inner loops for a matrix of size m x n yields a total work proportional to the total number of elements. Thus, the time complexity is O(m * n).
data.space_summary: The auxiliary space complexity is O(1) because we only store four boundary integer pointers and the traversal index variables, ignoring the memory required for the output list itself.
data.takeaway: When traversing structured grids or matrices in specific geometric patterns, maintain explicit boundary pointers (top, bottom, left, right) and shrink them dynamically after completing each full edge.
mistakes: Forgetting to check if top <= bottom or left <= right before executing the inner loops for the bottom and left traversals, which can cause duplicate element processing in matrices with odd dimensions or single rows/columns.
Incorrectly updating boundary variables (e.g., incrementing left instead of decrementing right), leading to infinite loops.
Confusing matrix dimensions m (rows) and n (columns) when initializing boundary pointers.
